newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS -Where would you put $100 million?.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS -Where would you put $100 million?.

text.p: World bond markets might be in for a rocky ride next year, but the most promising returns are to be found in...Italy, or is it Britain, Denmark, France, Japan, the U.S. or even South Africa?
Reuters asked a dozen London fixed income experts to choose one market where they would invest a $100 million Christmas windfall.
Favoured markets spanned nine countries in five continents. The reasons were as varied as the bonds they chose, but one common theme was that there were no sure bets out there.
This is what they said --
NIGEL RICHARDSON, BOND ECONOMIST, YAMAICHI INTERNATIONAL
"Italy has further to go. Italy is likely to participate in EMU (European Economic and Monetary Union) and very possibly even in 1999. We're not looking for any blow-up on that front."
JAMES MITCHELL, ECONOMIST, DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL

"Convergence is going to to be the theme in the markets and Italy is the only with substantial room for convergence. It is not necessarily going to be a smooth ride, but look for spreads to move down to 100 basis points by the end of next year." The BTP/Bund spread is currently around 175 basis points.
MICHAEL BURKE, ECONOMIST, CITIBANK

"I take a very cautious view of the bond markets at current valuations. They are severely overstreached. I would place my money somewhere...with expected rate cuts in the coming period -- Italy, Spain and Portugal. Of those I would put my money in the front end of the Italian curve."
MARK CAPLETON, INTERNATIONAL BOND STRATEGIST, BZW

"It's definitely time to sell Italy. I'd go for long Danish bonds. Denmark's single currency opt-out (from EMU) is being unfairly penalised by bond markets and its inflation history is tremendous. I also like Australian index-linked bonds, probably the longest ones out to 20 years."
STEPHEN LEWIS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, LONDON BOND BROKING
"If I had to pick only one I'd pick Denmark. Inflation is low, the budget deficit is no problem and there's room for more convergence between Denmark and Germany."
HUW ROBERTS, EUROPEAN STRATEGIST, NATWEST CAPITAL MARKETS

"I would adopt a very defensive trading stance in the first quarter, but over the second half of 1997 I would favour the British gilt market, towards the 10 year. At the moment things look a bit dire and there is more underperformance to go, but around June-time gilts should look cheaper."
BRONWYN CURTIS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, NOMURA INTERNATIONAL

"We'd be looking at the 10-year area of gilts. Changes in withholding tax will attract Japanese investors. Gilts are now one of the highest yielders in Europe, and all the bad news has been priced in. If EMU has problems, they will be in 1997 not 1998, so gilts will benefit as a safe haven from that."

GRAHAM MCDEVITT, SENIOR STRATEGIST, PARIBAS CAPITAL MARKETS "I'd pick the front end of the yield curve in France. Most international investors are very underweight France. The outlook for monetary policy is still neutral which is going to underpin the short end. But if I could trade my position I would trade out of France into Spain after the end of the first quarter."
STEPHEN HANNAH, HEAD OF RESEARCH, IBJ INTERNATIONAL

Treasuries will outperform Europe and Japan. He sees the U.S./German 10-year yield gap at parity by year-end versus 60 basis points now. "As we go into the second half of next year we'll see signficant underperformance in the U.S. economy after picking up in the first half. The Europeans meanwhile will begin to see stronger economic growth and the prospect of Bundesbank tightening and considerably heightened tensions over EMU."
ANDREW BEVAN, SENIOR BOND ECONOMIST, GOLDMAN SACHS

Goldman is bearish on bonds in 1997, with growth set to pick up and U.S. rates due to rise. Japan could be an unusual haven. "We're overweight Japan. We think the dollar/yen rate is close to peaking and we're going into there with a bearish view (generally). Japan will be somewhat sheltered."
BILL O'NEILL, MARKET STRATEGIST, HSBC JAMES CAPEL

"It is going to be a difficult year in the bond markets. So on the basis of being a total contrarian, I would put my money into South African bonds. They are the highest yielding of the developed world and it has had a dreadful year with pressure on the rand and the liquidity squeeze. The market has taken an overly aggressive, apocalyptic view."
-- Seasons Greetings, International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 6176
